stem: A thinly traded bond has no price on one day in an otherwise complete daily series used for a risk report. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Replace the missing price with the average price over the whole sample
Replace the missing daily return with the mean daily return
Forward-fill the last available price, with a limit on how many days can be filled
explanation: If an instrument did not trade, its last observed price is the best available mark. A fill limit prevents stale prices from masking a genuine data problem.

rationale.A: Incorrect. A full-sample average uses future information and can sit far from the current price, creating two fake large returns.
rationale.B: Incorrect. A zero price creates a -100% return followed by an infinite one.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Filling with the mean return invents data and understates volatility.
rationale.D: Correct. ffill(limit=...) carries the last mark forward for short gaps only.

stem: A stock closes at 90.00 the day before a 3-for-1 split and at 31.20 on the split's effective date. After correctly adjusting the history, the split-day return is:
explanation: Divide pre-split prices by the split ratio: 90.00 / 3 = 30.00. The adjusted return is 31.20 / 30.00 − 1 = 4.00%.

rationale.A: Incorrect. This is the raw, unadjusted return 31.20 / 90.00 − 1, a mechanical artefact of the split.
rationale.C: Incorrect. This adjusts with a ratio of 2 (90 / 2 = 45) instead of 3.
rationale.D: Incorrect. This divides the post-split price by 3 as well, adjusting the wrong side of the split.

stem: A Series is `[10, NaN, NaN, NaN, 11, NaN]`. How many NaN values remain after `s.ffill(limit=2)`?
explanation: The run of three NaNs after 10 is filled for only two positions, leaving the third as NaN. The final NaN after 11 is filled. One NaN remains.

rationale.A: Incorrect. This ignores the limit; unlimited ffill would fill all four.
rationale.B: Incorrect. The trailing NaN after 11 is also filled (it is a gap of one), so only one remains.
rationale.D: Incorrect. This is the count before filling.

verify: const s=[10,null,null,null,11,null]; let last=null, run=0; const out=s.map(v=>{ if(v!==null){last=v;run=0;return v;} run++; return (last!==null && run<=2)?last:null; }); return out.filter(v=>v===null).length;

stem: In a sample of eight daily returns, a bad print creates a +25% return. Its ordinary z-score is only about 2.5, but its robust z-score (median and MAD) is above 40. Why do the two measures disagree so much?
options: The outlier itself inflates the mean and standard deviation, shrinking its own ordinary z-score, while the median and MAD are barely affected
Robust z-scores always exaggerate values by the factor 1.4826
Ordinary z-scores cannot be computed when the data contain a positive outlier
The MAD is larger than the standard deviation, which makes robust z-scores larger
explanation: With few observations, one extreme value dominates the sample mean and standard deviation (masking). The median and median absolute deviation are resistant to a small number of extreme values, so the outlier stands out clearly.

rationale.A: Correct. Masking: the outlier pulls up the mean and blows up the standard deviation used to judge it.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 1.4826 scales the MAD to be comparable to a standard deviation under normality; it does not exaggerate scores.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Ordinary z-scores can always be computed; they are just distorted by the outlier.
rationale.D: Incorrect. Here the MAD is much smaller than the inflated standard deviation, which is why robust scores are larger.
